entry: Traditional first dynasty in Chinese historiography. A majority of Chinese archaeologists regard it as historical and identify it with the Erlitou culture (c. 1900–1500 BC), while many Western historians and Sinologists consider it legendary or unsubstantiated. Tradition holds that [[Yu the Great]] founded it and that the [[Shang dynasty]] succeeded it. No contemporaneous records mention the Xia; the earliest references occur in the *Book of Documents*, whose oldest chapters report speeches from the early Western Zhou period. Estimated dates vary: the traditional chronology gives 2205–1766 BC, a chronology based on the Bamboo Annals gives 1989–1558 BC, and the Xia–Shang–Zhou Chronology Project, commissioned by the Chinese government in 1996, proposed 2070–1600 BC. The *Shiji* of [[Sima Qian]] ties the dynasty's origins to flood control on the [[Yellow River]], in which Yu's father Gun failed and Yu succeeded.

Sub-provincial city in southeastern [[Fujian]], China, on the [[Taiwan Strait]] (pop., 2020: 5,163,970). Historically romanized as Amoy, after the pronunciation in the Zhangzhou dialect of Hokkien, it covers 1,700.61 sq km and is one of China's original four special economic zones, opened to foreign investment under [[Deng Xiaoping]]'s Opening Up Policy in the early 1980s. Its seaport, the Port of Xiamen, is ranked the seventh-largest container port in China. The Kinmen Islands, administered by Taiwan, lie less than 6 km away across Xiamen Bay. The city is home to several major universities, including Xiamen University, and is among the top 40 cities in the world by scientific research as tracked by the Nature Index.

Two-player strategy board game originating in China, commonly known in English as Chinese chess. The object is to checkmate the enemy general, and the game is widely played in China and Vietnam, where it is called *cờ tướng*. Xiangqi belongs to the same family as [[Chess]] and shogi, and its pieces sit on the intersections of a board nine lines wide and ten lines long, as in [[Go (game)|Go]]. Distinctive features include the cannon, which must jump over another piece to capture; a rule prohibiting the two generals from facing each other directly; and the river and palace zones, which restrict some pieces. Each player controls 16 pieces, identified by [[Chinese characters]] written in ink. Pieces may be made of wood, horn, bone, [[Ivory|ivory]] or, in more expensive sets, [[Jade|jade]].

Chinese multinational technology company headquartered in [[Beijing]], known for consumer electronics, software and electric vehicles. Founded in 2010 by Lei Jun and six associates, it released its first smartphone in August 2011. It was the third-largest smartphone seller in the world as of 2025, behind Apple and Samsung, and it has been called the "Apple of China." Its products include televisions, wearables, air purifiers and [[Unmanned aerial vehicle|unmanned aerial vehicles]], linked through an [[Internet of things]] ecosystem. The company ranked 232nd on the Fortune Global 500.

Autonomous region of northwestern China and the largest province-level division by area, with about 25 million inhabitants. It borders Afghanistan, India, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Mongolia, Pakistan, Russia and Tajikistan. High mountain ranges, including the [[Tian Shan]], divide it into the Dzungarian Basin in the north and the Tarim Basin in the south, and only about 9.7% of the land is fit for human habitation. The best-known route of the [[Silk Road]] ran through the territory. It came under [[Qing dynasty]] rule in the 18th century, became part of the People's Republic of China after the [[Chinese Civil War]], and was made an autonomous region in 1955. Oil and mineral reserves make it China's largest natural-gas-producing region. According to some, the government's ongoing human rights abuses against [[Uyghurs]] and other minorities amount to genocide; Chinese authorities describe their policies as essential for stability.

Tribal confederation of nomadic peoples on the eastern [[Eurasian Steppe]], active from the 3rd century BC to the late 1st century AD according to ancient Chinese sources. [[Modu Chanyu]], supreme leader after 209 BC, founded the Xiongnu Empire, which dominated the steppes of East Asia from the Mongolian Plateau. Relations with Chinese dynasties alternated between peace, war and subjugation. After a long conflict with the [[Han dynasty]], the confederation split in two, and large numbers of Xiongnu were resettled within Han borders. Their descendants intermixed with the [[Han Chinese]] and founded short-lived states in northern China, including Han-Zhao, Xia and Northern Liang, during the Sixteen Kingdoms period. By the 7th century the Xiongnu had completely integrated into Chinese society. Whether their name is cognate with that of the [[Huns]] remains disputed.

Order of marine arthropods related to [[Arachnid|arachnids]], commonly known as [[Horseshoe crab|horseshoe crabs]]. The group first appears in the fossil record in the Early [[Ordovician]], around 480 million years ago, and today has only four living species. Its members have changed little over hundreds of millions of years, and modern horseshoe crabs look almost identical to prehistoric genera, making them living fossils. The most notable difference between ancient and modern forms is that the abdominal segments of adult modern species are fused into a single unit. Modern xiphosurans reach up to 60 cm (24 in) in length, while many Paleozoic species were 1 to 3 cm (0.39 to 1.18 in) long. The name comes from Greek words meaning "sword" and "tail," referring to the sword-like telson.

Chinese Buddhist monk, scholar, traveler and translator. Born near [[Luoyang]] in [[Henan]], he was ordained at Chengdu and later went to Chang'an, where he resolved to visit India for original Sanskrit texts. From 629 to 645 he traveled overland to the Indian subcontinent, defying a ban on travel abroad, and he studied at Nalanda University in present-day [[Bihar]] under the monk Śīlabhadra. He sought to bring at least 657 Indian texts to China, and he translated 75 distinct sections of a total of 1,335 chapters, including some of the most important Mahayana scriptures. [[Emperor Taizong of Tang]] encouraged him to write the travelogue *Records of the Western Regions*, a source on 7th-century India and Central Asia that inspired the novel *Journey to the West*.

Chinese Confucian philosopher of the late Warring States period, often ranked as the third great Confucian after [[Confucius]] and [[Mencius]]. Born in the state of Zhao, he studied at the Jixia Academy in Qi and later taught there. His students [[Han Fei]] and [[Li Si]] had important political careers, though some of their Legalist views conflicted with his. He is best known for the claim that human nature is evil, which set him against Mencius, who held human nature to be good. For Xunzi, [[Education|education]] and [[Ritual|ritual]] were the means of correcting human nature. Misreadings of his views led to his gradual dismissal from the Tang dynasty onward, and Mencius overtook him when Neo-Confucianism emerged in the 10th century. Scholars reassessed his thought from the 20th century onward.

Sugar alcohol also called birch sugar, because it can be extracted from birch wood. The name derives from the Greek word for "wood." It is a colorless or white crystalline solid, and of the common sugar alcohols only sorbitol is more soluble in water. Xylitol is used as a food additive and sugar substitute, with the European Union code E967, and is considered safe for humans in the United States. Replacing sugar with xylitol may promote better dental health, but evidence is lacking that xylitol itself prevents cavities. It is severely toxic to [[Dog|dogs]].

Percussion instrument of wooden bars struck with mallets, each bar an idiophone tuned to a pitch of a [[Scale (music)|musical scale]]. The name comes from Greek words meaning "wood" and "sound." The term may broadly include instruments such as the marimba and balafon, but in the [[Orchestra|orchestra]] it refers specifically to a chromatic instrument with a higher pitch range and drier timbre than the marimba. Xylophones originated independently in ancient Africa and Southeast Asia, where many instruments use pentatonic or heptatonic scales. Their use in Western classical music grew in the 19th century; Camille Saint-Saëns wrote for it in *Danse Macabre* (1874). Contemporary concert xylophones typically have 30 to 44 rosewood bars suspended over metal tube resonators.

Worldwide youth organization based in Vernier, Canton of [[Geneva]], [[Switzerland]], with more than 64 million beneficiaries in 120 countries. It was founded in London on June 6, 1844, by George Williams as the Young Men's Christian Association, with the stated aim of putting Christian values into practice by developing a healthy body, mind and spirit. It is a non-governmental federation of independent local associations, and its programs vary by nation but are based on the Paris Basis. Local branches offer athletic facilities, classes, Christian programs and humanitarian work. The YWCA is independent, although some local and national associations have merged with YMCA groups.

Class of supernatural beings and spirits in Japanese folklore, including shapeshifters, ghosts, demons and tricksters. *Yōkai* may be mischievous, helpful or malevolent, and they often appear as animal-like figures, possessed objects or humanoids. Examples include the kappa, which resembles a turtle, and the tengu, which is commonly depicted with wings. Some academics and [[Shinto]] practitioners regard *yōkai* and most *kami*, which are generally more beneficent, as ultimately the same type of nature spirit. In the [[Edo period]], artists such as Toriyama Sekien invented many new *yōkai*, and several of these are today mistakenly thought to come from traditional folklore. The Japanese name transliterates the Chinese term *yāoguài*; its kanji both mean "suspicious, doubtful."

American web portal based in Sunnyvale, California, known for its [[Search engine|search engine]], Yahoo Search, and for services including Yahoo Mail, Yahoo News and Yahoo Finance. Jerry Yang and David Filo established the company in January 1994, and it was one of the pioneers of the early Internet era in the 1990s. Its use declined in the 2010s, when some of its services were discontinued and it lost market share to [[Facebook]] and [[Google]]. The operating company, Yahoo! Inc., is 90% owned by Apollo Global Management and 10% by Verizon.

Ancient Semitic deity in the southeastern [[Canaan|Levant]] who became the national god of the Iron Age kingdoms of Israel-Samaria and Judah. Most scholars favor a southern origin for Yahweh worship, which dates to at least the early [[Iron Age]] and possibly the late [[Bronze Age]]. Israelite religion derived from the Canaanite religion and included deities such as [[El (deity)|El]], Asherah and [[Baal]]. Yahweh likely became conflated with El and took his place as head of the pantheon, and El-linked epithets such as *ʾĒl Šadday* came to be applied to him alone. According to a pious interpretation, Jews began substituting other Hebrew words, chiefly *ădōnāy* ("my lords"), for the name during the Second Temple period, and by the destruction of the Second Temple in 70 CE its original pronunciation was forgotten. Yahweh is also invoked in an Imperial Aramaic papyrus from [[Ancient Egypt]].

Long-haired domesticated Asian [[Cattle|cattle]] (*Bos grunniens*) found throughout the Himalayan region, the [[Tibetan Plateau]], [[Tajikistan]], the Pamir Mountains, and north to [[Mongolia]] and [[Siberia]]. It descends from the wild yak (*Bos mutus*). Domesticated about 5,000–10,000 years ago on the eastern Qinghai-Tibetan Plateau, the yak is adapted to altitudes of 3,000–5,500 meters, with thick [[Wool|wool]], large lungs and heart, and a low heart rate. Around 14 million domestic yaks exist, more than 90 percent of them in China, Mongolia and Russia. They provide milk, meat, wool, hides, dung for fuel and fertilizer, and transport. The wild yak, estimated at about 15,000 individuals, is classified as vulnerable.

Capital and largest city of the [[Sakha Republic]], Russia, about 450 km (280 mi) south of the [[Arctic Circle]]. Fueled by mining, it had a population of 355,443 at the 2021 census. Its average annual temperature is −8.0 °C (17.6 °F), and a record low of −64.4 °C (−83.9 °F) has been recorded. It is the coldest city of more than 200,000 people in the world, though some smaller towns in the region are colder. Yakutsk is the largest city built on continuous [[Permafrost|permafrost]], and it is a major port on the [[Lena River]].

Members of transnational organized crime syndicates originating in [[Japan]], also called *gokudō* or the Japanese mafia. Their strict codes of conduct and unconventional rituals include *yubitsume*, the amputation of the left little finger. Membership peaked at 184,100 members and quasi-members in 1963. By 2025 there were only 9,400 members and 8,200 quasi-members, as young people stopped joining and legal and social changes discouraged membership. The yakuza still regularly engage in criminal activities, and no strict prohibition on membership exists, although many laws target their revenue and liability.

Private Ivy League research university in [[New Haven, Connecticut|New Haven]], [[Connecticut]]. Founded in 1701 as the Collegiate School by Congregationalist clergy, it is the fourth-oldest institution of higher education in the United States and one of nine colonial colleges chartered before the [[American Revolution]]. It awarded the first PhD in the United States in 1864 and organized as a university in 1887. Yale comprises fifteen constituent schools, including Yale Law School and the Yale Graduate School of Arts and Sciences. Its endowment was valued at $54.5 billion in 2025, the second-largest among educational institutions, and its library holds more than 15 million volumes. Alumni include five U.S. presidents, and the university's athletic teams compete as the Yale [[Bulldog|Bulldogs]].

Wartime meeting of the heads of government of the United States, the United Kingdom and the Soviet Union, held February 4–11, 1945, near Yalta in [[Crimea]]. [[Franklin D. Roosevelt]], Winston Churchill and [[Joseph Stalin]] met to plan the postwar reorganization of Germany and Europe, with the aim of a peace that gave self-determination to the liberated peoples of Europe. It was the second of three major wartime meetings of the Big Three, after the Tehran Conference in November 1943 and before the Potsdam Conference in July 1945. Its decisions included four zones of occupation for Germany and a framework for the United Nations. Because the [[Cold War]] divided Europe within a few years, the conference became a subject of intense controversy.

Common name for plant species in the genus *Dioscorea* that form edible tubers, though some species in the genus are toxic. Yams are perennial herbaceous vines native to Africa, Asia and the Americas, and they are cultivated in many temperate and tropical regions. About 10 species have been domesticated, and the tubers serve as a primary source of carbohydrates in tropical diets. Africa accounts for more than 97 percent of world output, which reached 88 million tonnes in 2022, and [[Nigeria]] produces about 70 percent. Yams rank fourth among root and tuber crops worldwide, after potatoes, [[Cassava]] and sweet potatoes. The growing cycle lasts 8–11 months, and post-harvest losses can reach 20–30 percent. Nigeria's New Yam Festival celebrates the harvest.

Two battleships of the Imperial Japanese Navy, *Yamato* and *Musashi*, which were the heaviest battleships ever constructed. Displacing nearly 72,000 long tons at full load, they carried nine 460 mm (18.1 in) guns, the largest naval artillery ever fitted to a warship. Because of the threat from U.S. submarines and aircraft carriers, they spent most of their careers at bases in [[Brunei]], Truk and Kure. *Musashi* was sunk by air strikes during the [[Battle of Leyte Gulf|Battle of Leyte Gulf]] in October 1944, and *Yamato* by air strikes in April 1945 during Operation Ten-Go. A third hull was converted into the [[Aircraft carrier|aircraft carrier]] *Shinano*, which was torpedoed by a U.S. submarine in November 1944.

Late Copper Age to early Bronze Age archaeological culture of the Pontic–Caspian steppe, dating to 3300–2600 BC. Also known as the Pit Grave or Ochre Grave culture, it takes its name from the Russian word for "related to pits," describing burials in simple pit chambers beneath tumuli. Its economy rested on [[Animal husbandry|animal husbandry]], fishing and foraging, as well as the manufacture of [[Ceramic|ceramics]], tools and weapons. Its people were nomadic or semi-nomadic, riding horses and traveling by wheeled carts and wagons. The widely accepted Kurgan hypothesis links the culture to speakers of Proto-Indo-European, whose migrations gave rise to the Indo-European languages.

Second-largest tributary of the [[Ganges]] by discharge and the longest tributary in India, flowing 1,376 kilometers (855 mi) from the Yamunotri Glacier in Uttarakhand to its confluence at Prayagraj. The river drains an area of 366,223 sq km and supplies nearly 57 million people; it accounts for more than 70 percent of [[Delhi]]'s water supply. Its confluence with the Ganges at Triveni Sangam is the site of the [[Kumbh Mela]], a Hindu festival held every 12 years. In [[Hinduism]] the Yamuna is venerated as a goddess, the daughter of the sun god Surya and sister of Yama, the god of death. The 22-kilometer stretch from the Wazirabad barrage to the Okhla barrage in Delhi is less than 2 percent of its length but accounts for nearly 80 percent of the river's pollution.

Russian technology company that provides internet services including a web browser, search engine, cloud computing, web mapping, streaming media, online shopping and ridesharing. Founded by Arkady Volozh, it launched its first product, a search engine, in 1997. Yandex Search holds an estimated 72 percent of the market in [[Russia]], and Yandex Taxi is the largest ridesharing company there. The company also develops generative AI models and the Alice virtual assistant. Under international sanctions related to the Russian invasion of Ukraine, its Dutch holding company, Nebius Group, sold the Russian assets in July 2024 to a consortium of Russian investors.
